1:
John Calvin explains why the chapter turns where it does: the calamities described might have terrified the godly into despair, so consolation was necessary. He notes that the prophet keeps the figure with which the previous chapter closed, Jerusalem consumed as by a single conflagration, and now shows what will spring from the burnt ground. Adam Clarke states the same movement as the chapter's argument: a slender twig from the root of an old withered stem, weak at first and yet to become fruitful and mighty. Keil and Delitzsch put it as a law rather than a picture — in the humble beginning lies a power that will carry it to a great height by a steady process, the twig becoming a tree with a crown laden with fruit, so that humiliation is followed by exaltation.

Who the rod is was disputed, and two voices answer the same objection differently. John Gill reports that a Jewish commentator took it for Hezekiah, and dismisses that on chronology, since he was already ten or twelve years old when the words were spoken; many Jewish writers, ancient and modern, own the Messiah here. Calvin rejects the same opinion on other grounds: when Hezekiah was born the house of David still had a flourishing reputation and royalty belonged to it, whereas the prophecy requires a stump. John Wesley presses the noun: it means a trunk cut off from the root, so the Messiah was to be born of the royal house in a most forlorn condition, a tree felled with nothing left but a stump underground. He also draws out the choice of name — the prophet does not say of David but of Jesse, a private and mean person, to intimate that at Christ's birth the royal family would be reduced to its primitive obscurity. Matthew Henry adds that some have thought the word here referred to in the evangelist's remark that the Messiah should be called a Nazarene.

On the Spirit resting, Delitzsch reads a formal act: the Lord acknowledges him, and consecrates and equips him for his great work with the seven spirits. Charles Ellicott hears the phrase looking both ways at once. It was the spirit of the Lord that made men heroes and judges of old, and the same spirit descending on Jesus by which men were taught to see the token that he was the Christ of God. But what is promised here is more than the heroic daring of a Jephthah or a Samson: the future king was to be a David and a Solomon in one. Gill takes the resting of the Spirit as proof that the kingdom is spiritual, and finds in the verse a clear proof of the trinity of Persons, the Spirit being one Jehovah with the Father yet distinct from him and from the Son; Christ was filled with the Spirit from the womb, and the Spirit descended on him at his baptism.

Whether the titles that follow should be distinguished divides the voices in method rather than doctrine. Wesley says it is not needful to distinguish the first two exactly, since it is enough that they are the qualifications of a governor and a teacher, signifying perfect knowledge and sound judgment; he does separate the next pair, counsel as prudence to give good advice and might as courage to execute it, and defines the fear at the end as a fear of reverence, a care to please and a lothness to offend. Ellicott and Delitzsch treat the list as an ordered endowment rather than overlapping words; Gill takes each as qualifying Christ for a distinct part of his office. Calvin insists that with this verse the prophet begins to speak of Christ plainly, the earlier consolation being given under a figure only so that the contrast between the burning of the wood and its springing up anew might be fully seen.
3:
The first clause turns on a verb of smelling, and no two voices render it alike. Charles Ellicott prefers that he shall draw his breath in the fear of the Lord, so that it is the air in which he lives, while reporting the alternative that he shall find a sweet savour in it; the noun our version gives as understanding means primarily scent, organ or object of perception. Keil and Delitzsch render it that the fear of Jehovah is fragrance to him, and reject two scholars who made the smelling a keen judicial insight into that fear, since the verb with this preposition will not carry it. John Calvin takes the verb actively and thinks that sense better, so that shrewd discernment is numbered among the gifts of the Spirit: Christ will be so quick that he need not learn from what he hears or sees. John Wesley alone declines the figure and reads a moral rule, that he shall not judge rashly or partially but considerately and justly, as the fear of God obliges every judge.

The judgment is described by contrast. Ellicott sets it against the corrupt judges Isaiah had already portrayed, so the poor whom they trampled become the true King's special charge, and adds the difference between kings who judge by appearance and one who knows what is in man. John Gill makes the poor the poor in spirit, hungering after righteousness. Calvin narrows it further and says so openly: the prophet points out the persons to whom the grace of Christ strictly belongs, those humbled by a conviction of their poverty who have laid aside the proud dispositions that swell men's minds, so that Christ is guardian not of all men whatsoever but of such as know themselves destitute of every good.

Two conjectures are offered on the smiting that follows, from different directions. Adam Clarke reports an emendation reading not the rod of his mouth but the blast of it, from a root meaning to blow, and calls it ingenious and probable: the Greek and Chaldee rendering by the word of his mouth suits the correction better than the received text, and blast makes an exact parallel to the breath of the lips. Ellicott leaves the rod alone and emends the object, since a slight alteration gives smite the tyrant, which parallels the ungodly of the next clause better than the earth does; failing that, he takes the earth for the rulers who are for the time supreme in it. Wesley makes the rod the word, the sceptre by whose preaching the world was subdued, and draws the point he thinks the verse exists to make, that Christ's kingdom is not of this world.

The girdle raises a textual question and a defence of the text. Clarke observes that all the ancient versions but one use two different words in the two halves of the line, thinks it improbable that the prophet would repeat one word when an obvious synonym lay to hand, and concludes that the tautology arose from a transcriber's mistake; the sense he takes to be that zeal for justice and truth will make the King strong in the work he undertakes. Ellicott answers directly: the repetition has needlessly offended some fastidious critics, but emphasis by iteration is quite in Isaiah's manner, and the doubling may imply an upper and a lower girdle as the sign of complete equipment. He adds that the loins girt about with truth in the apostle's armour are probably an allusion here, the armour of Christ's followers being like his own. Calvin reads the word as a royal emblem rather than a garment, since the prophet is representing Christ wearing the ensigns of royalty, and supports it from the passage where taking away the authority of kings is described as God ungirding them: to be girded is to be exalted to royal authority.
6:
Whether the peaceable kingdom is about animals or men is the question under all four verses. John Gill reads it wholly of the Church: the cow and the bear feed together in one church state, the one having dispensed the milk of the divine word and the other worried the lambs of Christ, now of one nature and without fear. John Wesley gives both senses at once: the creatures shall be restored to the innocency they had before the fall, and men of fierce disposition so transformed by grace as to become gentle. Charles Ellicott insists the animal world is genuinely included, and finds it significant of the prophet's sympathy that he thinks of it as sharing in redemption: rapine and cruelty even there were marks to him of an imperfect order, and the very instincts of the brute creation are to be changed. John Calvin holds both together: the prophet ascends from the body to the head and descends again, since Christ reigns not for himself but for those who believe; but the discourse looks beyond even that, amounting to a promise of a blessed restoration of the world, the order that obtained before man's apostasy.

Adam Clarke sets the passage beside its pagan parallels, the idea of a renewed golden age being much the same in oriental writers as in the Greek and Latin poets — wild beasts growing tame, serpents and poisonous herbs harmless, all peace and plenty — and quotes a Roman eclogue in which the serpent's brood dies, the ground refuses noxious plants, and the flocks no longer fear the great lions. Keil and Delitzsch mark structure rather than substance: the righteous conduct of the Son of David has been described, and now the peace prevailing under his government, extending even to the animal world and consequent on a knowledge of God become universal.

The serpent's den produces the sharpest disagreement of detail. Clarke reports a reading from the Targum and a Jewish commentator on which the phrase means not the den but the pupil of the serpent's eye: when the creature lies in the mouth of his hole his eyes sparkle, and the child, taking the glitter for crystal or a precious stone, puts out his hand to seize it — dangerous at any other time but safe in the days of the Messiah. Ellicott keeps the hole and identifies the creatures, the cobra and the great viper, and measures the promise by present feeling: the sight of a child beside such a hole would now make its mother scream with terror. Calvin draws a different inference from the same danger: men dread the poison of serpents only because they do not deserve that God should place every part of the world under their control, and since the creatures are permitted to injure even infants, this shows the whole race stained with pollution from the womb.

At the close the voices differ over who does no hurt. Ellicott allows that the pronoun may refer back to the beasts, so that the prophet sees a restored Eden in which the fiercest brutes have lost their fierceness, but notes that the words equally bear a general statement that none shall hurt or destroy; the holy mountain he identifies with the mountain of the Lord's house in its future glory. Calvin declares plainly for men: they will have laid aside the depravity that naturally dwells in them and be inclined of their own accord to do right — and he means believers truly regenerated, since the hypocrites mixed among the elect are like the sons of the bondwoman, whom God will cast out at the proper time. Gill sets the fulfilment after the destruction of antichrist, when the saints will no longer be harassed by men like those creatures for cruelty or cunning; Wesley locates the mountain in Zion, in the church.
10:
When the ensign was or will be raised is the first dispute. Matthew Henry finds a partial accomplishment already: the great things God did for Hezekiah served as an ensign inviting neighbouring nations to enquire after the wonders done in the land, and on that errand the king of Babylon's ambassadors came. Adam Clarke will allow nothing of the kind, saying this part of the chapter contains a prophecy that certainly remains yet to be accomplished. John Gill places it in the ministration of the Gospel, where Christ is held forth as the only Saviour, and the gathering continues until all his people are brought in. John Calvin locates the difficulty rather than the date: that the Gentiles who formerly abhorred the Jews should bow before their King seemed incredible, and the promise was ridiculed for centuries, since such a gathering might have been looked for while the kingdom flourished and not after it was cut down — yet cut down it had to be.

On the root itself Charles Ellicott ties the verse back to the chapter's opening, and pictures the new shoot of the fallen tree growing like a stately palm on the heights, a signal round which distant nations might rally; the title is applied to the glorified Christ in the Revelation, and the verb for seeking implies the particular seeking of wisdom and illumination. Clarke reports a manuscript variant giving the present participle, so the root is said to stand and to have stood as an ensign. John Wesley reads the promised rest as the resting-place, the temple or church, whose glory will exceed the tabernacle's but be spiritual, in plentiful effusions of the gifts and graces of the Spirit. Keil and Delitzsch frame the rest of the chapter as a series of questions: since the nation for which this king arises will by then be scattered far from its native land, how can he reign in the midst of it?

What earlier deliverance the second recovery is measured against divides the voices cleanly. Ellicott says the first time is obviously the Exodus, when from extremest misery they entered on their life as a nation, and what happened then is to be reproduced yet more wonderfully; the list of countries rests partly on a dispersion already begun. Calvin agrees and gives the reason for the reminder: recalling a past deliverance keeps the elect from doubting that God is as able to deliver them now as their fathers found him in Egypt. Wesley takes the first deliverance to be the return from Babylon, from which it follows that this second must belong to the days of the Messiah. Clarke leaves the question aside for the text, reporting that many manuscripts read the divine name differently in the opening clause, and passing on a Jewish commentator's identification of the islands of the sea with the Roman and Turkish empires.

The gathering itself is read at two levels. Gill and Wesley take the nations broadly, Jews and Gentiles together, the outcasts those driven from their land into foreign parts. Ellicott finds a detail the versions lose: the outcasts are masculine and the dispersed feminine, so the prophet implies that in Israel and Judah alike both sexes should share in the restoration. Calvin says the language is metaphorical and will bear two senses, either that God will terrify the adversaries so they dare not prevent the return, or that he signals to the exiles not to hesitate; and he turns it into use, that as an ensign is lifted in an army so soldiers may assemble and each keep his place, so an ensign is held out to us, which is the gospel. Delitzsch reads the verse as raising the next question in his sequence, the mention of Israel and Judah together calling to mind the rent in the nation's unity and prompting the enquiry whether it will continue.
13:
The healing of the old division is read at three widths. Charles Ellicott keeps it national: the prophet's vision would have been incomplete without unity, and looking back he saw almost from the first a deep cleavage between north and south, a chasm widening century by century, which in the times of the Christ the sense of unity should outweigh; he connects the hope with Hezekiah's own efforts after unity. John Calvin widens it to religion, dwelling on the allaying of domestic quarrels so that the children of Abraham may cease to harass one another and unite in the same worship, a disgraceful thing while it lasted. John Gill widens it further, taking in whatever envy has subsisted between Jew and Gentile, and then whatever has appeared in one Christian church or denomination against another, all to cease when the Gospel takes hold in its power and purity.

What follows is a picture of conquest, its first phrase obscure. Ellicott warns that our version is ambiguous and half suggests the Philistines will carry the returning Israelites on their shoulders; the Greek went further, making it their speeding on wings in the ships of the aliens. What is meant, he says, is that the exiles swoop down like a bird of prey upon the shoulder of the Philistines, that word being used of the shape of the seaward-sloping country they occupied. Keil and Delitzsch treat the verse as the next of the chapter's questions: given the warlike Philistines, the predatory nomads of the east, the unbrotherly Edomites, the boasting Moabites and the cruel Ammonites, will they not weaken the new Israel as they did the old?

The drying of the water is disputed in nearly every term. On the tongue, Calvin explains the figure — when the sea penetrates the land there is a resemblance to a man putting out his tongue — and Wesley reports that geographers give the name to promontories shooting into the sea. Ellicott prefers bay or gulf and identifies it as the Gulf of Suez, so that the prophet is picturing another marvel like the passage of the Red Sea. What the river is divides them more sharply. Ellicott grants that the word is the one commonly used of the Euphrates and that most commentators take it so, but notes that elsewhere it stands in parallel with the sea of Egypt and there means the Nile, so that meaning may well be accepted; Calvin and Wesley take the Nile without hesitation, Wesley adding that the seven streams are what it is famous for, and Gill reports two Jewish commentators for the same. Clarke works on the verbs, reporting that the Chaldee gives a word meaning shall desolate, and that the Greek, Latin and Chaldee read a form meaning shall make it passable, supplying a pronoun the sense requires though no manuscript confirms it.

At the highway the voices converge on the same comparison, then part over its scope. Ellicott describes the thing itself, the raised embanked road Eastern kings built for the march of armies, and sees such a road stretching across the plains of Mesopotamia, so that it is to the second restoration what the crossing of the sea had been to the first. Calvin makes a general point about expectation: the people would perceive in the deliverance from Babylon the same power they had seen in the deliverance from Egypt, God having opened a way through seas and untrodden deserts and the Jordan, so that what the Lord has once performed we may look for again. Gill takes the highway into his own scheme of prophecy: when the Mahometan, Pagan and Papal kingdoms are destroyed with their several religions, the way of truth and holiness will lie open to the remnant of the Lord's people, who will walk in it and not err.
